title: What keeps a sliding puck going?
hook: Things stop when you stop pushing. Or is something else stopping them?

knows: speeds in m/s and distances in metres

misconception: Keeping an object moving at a constant speed needs a continuing force; without a push, motion dies away by itself.
objective: The learner can explain that an object keeps its speed when no net force acts, and that everyday objects stop because friction is a force acting on them.

claims.text: With no friction and no push, a puck moving at 2 m/s keeps moving at 2 m/s: it covers 2 m every second, 20 m in 10 s.
claims.source: Newton's first law: zero net force means zero acceleration, so velocity is constant; x = v t = 2 x 10 = 20 m. Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5.

claims.text: Kinetic friction slows a sliding puck at a steady rate mu g, so it stops after v / (mu g) seconds, having gone v^2 / (2 mu g).
claims.source: Dry kinetic friction model: friction force mu m g opposing motion, a = -mu g (Coulomb friction; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 6). x(t) = v t - mu g t^2 / 2 until v = 0.

claims.text: On the lanes, high friction (mu = 0.10) stops the puck in 2.0 m; medium (0.03) in 6.8 m; low (0.01) leaves it at about 1 m/s after 10 s, 15.1 m along.
The friction values (0.10, 0.03, 0.01, 0) are illustrative, not measurements of particular surfaces; a truly frictionless surface is an idealisation.
claims.source: Stated idealisation chosen by the builder so the four stopping distances fit one 20 m lane.

claims.text: A force changes motion; without one, motion carries on. Friction is the force that stops things in daily life.
claims.source: Newton, Principia (1687), Law I; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, ch. 5 and 6.

recall.question: A space probe far from any star or planet is coasting at 15 km/s with its engines off. What happens to its speed?
recall.why: With no force acting, nothing changes the motion; there is no friction in empty space to slow it.
